angle: angle 1 · a place and a time
title: Growing Up in 1972 America: The Forgotten Decade

scenes.text: People love to talk about the fifties and the sixties. But the seventies? They often get skipped, or remembered only for bad haircuts and disco. Yet if you were a kid in nineteen seventy-two, you know it was a wonderful time to grow up. It was a decade of freedom, Big Wheels, Saturday morning cartoons and long, lazy summers.
scenes.caption: THE FORGOTTEN DECADE

scenes.text: In nineteen seventy-two, the oldest baby boomers were in their mid-twenties, and the youngest were eight. A new generation of kids was right behind them. Families were a little smaller, houses were a little bigger, and the country was going through a lot of changes. But for a kid, life was mostly about the next bike ride.

So let's go back. Let's spend a year growing up in nineteen seventy-two America. Home, school, television, toys, cars and the big news of the year. If you were there, I think it's going to come rushing back.
scenes.caption: LET'S GO BACK

scenes.text: The house in nineteen seventy-two had a look all its own. Wood paneling on the walls. Shag carpet in harvest gold, avocado green or burnt orange. A kitchen with appliances in the same colors. A big console television, now often in color. And macrame plant hangers in the window.
scenes.caption: HARVEST GOLD

scenes.text: In nineteen seventy-two, about half of American homes had a color television, and the share was growing fast. Families still had just a few channels, usually the three networks and maybe a public station or a local independent. And there was still only one television in most houses, which led to a lot of arguments.
scenes.caption: COLOR TV

scenes.text: More mothers were working outside the home than ever before. By nineteen seventy-two, around four in ten married women held a job. That meant more kids came home from school to an empty house, with a key on a string around their neck. They called them latchkey kids, and they learned to make their own snacks.
scenes.caption: LATCHKEY KIDS

scenes.text: The family dinner was still a big deal, though. Hamburger Helper had just arrived in nineteen seventy-one, and it quickly became a weeknight favorite. Mothers made tuna casserole, sloppy joes, fish sticks and Shake 'n Bake chicken. And for dessert, there might be Jell-O with fruit in it, or a slice of Sara Lee cake from the freezer.
scenes.caption: HAMBURGER HELPER

scenes.text: And kids in seventy-two spent most of their time outside. Mothers sent them out in the morning and called them home for dinner. Nobody knew exactly where they were. They rode bikes miles from home, explored creeks and woods, built forts, and played ball in empty lots until the streetlights came on.
scenes.caption: UNTIL THE STREETLIGHTS

scenes.text: The bike of the moment was the Schwinn Sting-Ray, with its banana seat, high-rise handlebars and a sissy bar in the back. Some had a stick shift on the frame, like a sports car. Kids put baseball cards in the spokes with clothespins, so their bikes sounded like motorcycles.
scenes.caption: THE STING-RAY

scenes.text: Younger kids had the Big Wheel, a low plastic tricycle with a giant front wheel, made by Marx Toys. On a sidewalk or driveway, a Big Wheel made a roaring sound that every parent of the seventies still remembers. Kids raced them, crashed them, and spun them out in perfect skids.
scenes.caption: THE BIG WHEEL

scenes.text: In the summer, kids ran through sprinklers, played on Slip 'N Slides, and spent whole days at the public swimming pool. They drank from the garden hose. Ice cream trucks came down the street playing music. And if you had a quarter, you could get a Bomb Pop or a Push-Up.
scenes.caption: THE GARDEN HOSE

scenes.text: Kids also had a lot of jobs. Paper routes, mowing lawns, babysitting, and shoveling snow in winter. A paperboy in nineteen seventy-two might earn ten or fifteen dollars a week, which felt like a fortune. He collected from each house on Friday, and learned exactly which neighbors tipped well and which didn't.
scenes.caption: THE PAPER ROUTE

scenes.text: School in seventy-two was changing. Many schools had new open classrooms, with no walls between them. Students used workbooks, filmstrips and overhead projectors. And many schools still smelled of the purple ink from the ditto machine. A fresh, damp ditto sheet was something kids would hold up to their noses.
scenes.caption: THE DITTO MACHINE

scenes.text: Kids carried metal lunch boxes with their favorite TV shows on them. The Partridge Family, The Brady Bunch, Scooby-Doo, Star Trek and The Waltons. At lunch, they traded snacks like Twinkies, Ding Dongs and Hostess fruit pies. And they drank milk from little cartons.
scenes.caption: THE LUNCH BOX

scenes.text: And in June of nineteen seventy-two, a new law called Title Nine was signed. It said that no one could be excluded from any school program that received federal money because of their sex. Within a few years, the number of girls playing high school sports multiplied. Many girls of the seventies were the first in their families to play on a real team.
scenes.caption: TITLE IX

scenes.text: Saturday morning was the most important time of the week. Kids woke up early, poured a giant bowl of sugary cereal, and sat on the floor in front of the television in their pajamas. Cap'n Crunch, Froot Loops, Lucky Charms and Count Chocula. Cartoons ran from seven until noon.
scenes.caption: SATURDAY MORNING

scenes.text: In nineteen seventy-two, kids watched Scooby-Doo, Fat Albert and the Cosby Kids, The Bugs Bunny Show, and The Flintstones. And there were short educational cartoons between the shows. Many grown-ups today can still sing every word of Schoolhouse Rock, which first aired in early nineteen seventy-three.
scenes.caption: SCOOBY-DOO

scenes.text: By noon, the cartoons ended, and kids were sent outside. That was the deal. Parents could sleep in on Saturday morning, and the kids got their cartoons. Then the afternoon belonged to the neighborhood.
scenes.caption: THAT WAS THE DEAL

scenes.text: Saturday afternoons might mean a matinee at the local movie theater. In nineteen seventy-two, the big movies were The Godfather, which most kids weren't allowed to see, and The Poseidon Adventure, which they were. Disney rereleased its classics, and kids saw Bambi, Lady and the Tramp or Pinocchio in a real theater for about a dollar.
scenes.caption: THE MATINEE

scenes.text: Evening television in nineteen seventy-two was some of the best ever made. All in the Family was the most-watched show in America. Sanford and Son was a new hit. And in the fall, two new shows started that would last for years. M*A*S*H and The Waltons.
scenes.caption: ALL IN THE FAMILY

scenes.text: Families watched The Mary Tyler Moore Show, The Carol Burnett Show and The Partridge Family. Kids were allowed to stay up for The Wonderful World of Disney on Sunday nights. And on weekday afternoons, a new version of The Price Is Right, hosted by Bob Barker, started that fall. It would run for decades.
scenes.caption: THE PRICE IS RIGHT

scenes.text: And in November of nineteen seventy-two, something new appeared in a few homes in Pennsylvania. A cable channel called Home Box Office. HBO. At the time, almost nobody noticed. It would one day change television completely.
scenes.caption: HBO, 1972

scenes.text: The toys of seventy-two were wonderful. Lite-Brite, Spirograph, Etch A Sketch and Lincoln Logs. Evel Knievel action figures were coming soon, and Hot Wheels raced down orange plastic tracks. Girls had Barbie and Holly Hobbie, and the Easy-Bake Oven, which baked a tiny cake with a light bulb.
scenes.caption: LITE-BRITE AND HOT WHEELS

scenes.text: And in nineteen seventy-two, two things appeared that would change the world. The Magnavox Odyssey, the first home video game console, which plugged into the television. And Pong, the arcade game made by a new company called Atari. Two paddles, one bouncing dot. It sounds simple, but kids lined up to play it.
scenes.caption: PONG

scenes.text: Kids also collected things. Baseball cards, with a flat pink stick of gum in every pack. Wacky Packages stickers that made fun of real products. Comic books from the spinning rack at the drugstore, for twenty cents each. And many kids kept their collections in shoeboxes under the bed, where many of them stayed for fifty years.
scenes.caption: IN A SHOEBOX

scenes.text: The family car of nineteen seventy-two was big. A station wagon with fake wood paneling on the sides and a rear-facing back seat. A Ford Country Squire, a Chevy Kingswood or an Oldsmobile Vista Cruiser. Gasoline was still about thirty-six cents a gallon. Nobody worried about it, yet.
scenes.caption: THE STATION WAGON

scenes.text: Seat belts were in the cars, but almost nobody wore them. Kids rolled around in the back, or lay in the cargo area looking out the back window. On long trips, they played the license plate game, counted cows, and fought over who was touching whom. And there was always a cooler with sandwiches and soda.
scenes.caption: NOBODY WORE SEAT BELTS

scenes.text: The radio played the hits of seventy-two. American Pie by Don McLean, which was number one in January. Lean on Me by Bill Withers. Alone Again by Gilbert O'Sullivan. I Can See Clearly Now, Brand New Key, and Song Sung Blue. Dad usually picked the station.
scenes.caption: AMERICAN PIE

scenes.text: Nineteen seventy-two was full of big news, much of which went over a kid's head. In February, President Nixon traveled to China, the first American president ever to visit. Families watched pictures of him walking on the Great Wall. It seemed impossible just a few years earlier.
scenes.caption: NIXON IN CHINA

scenes.text: In June, a small burglary happened at an office building in Washington called the Watergate. Most people paid little attention at the time. But it would grow into the biggest political scandal in American history, and two years later, President Nixon would resign. Kids of seventy-two would watch the hearings on TV the next summer.
scenes.caption: THE WATERGATE

scenes.text: That summer, swimmer Mark Spitz won seven gold medals at the Olympics, and his poster went up on bedroom walls across America. The war in Vietnam was winding down, and most American ground troops had come home. And in December, Apollo seventeen flew to the moon. Nobody knew it would be the last time humans walked there.
scenes.caption: THE LAST MOON LANDING

scenes.text: The seventies were also a time of worry. Cities were struggling. Factories were starting to close in some places. Prices were creeping up. And pollution had become a serious concern. The Environmental Protection Agency had been created in nineteen seventy, and the first Earth Day that same year had made kids aware of litter, smog and dirty rivers.
scenes.caption: A TIME OF WORRY

scenes.text: A famous television ad showed a Native American man shedding a single tear at a polluted highway. Keep America Beautiful, it said. Kids took it seriously. They picked up litter, collected cans for recycling, and lectured their parents about throwing trash out of the car window.
scenes.caption: KEEP AMERICA BEAUTIFUL

scenes.text: Looking back, nineteen seventy-two was the last year of a certain kind of innocence. The next year brought the oil crisis, gas lines and inflation. Watergate unfolded. But in seventy-two, gas was cheap, the moon was within reach, and a kid on a bike could ride all day and nobody worried.
scenes.caption: THE LAST INNOCENT YEAR

scenes.text: That's why so many people who grew up in the early seventies feel the decade has been forgotten. It doesn't have a neat image like the fifties. But it was the decade when kids had the most freedom of any generation, before video games moved inside and parents started to worry more.
scenes.caption: THE MOST FREEDOM

scenes.text: If you grew up in nineteen seventy-two, you remember it. The smell of the ditto sheet. The sound of the Big Wheel. Saturday morning cereal. American Pie on the car radio. It wasn't a forgotten decade to you. It was your childhood.
scenes.caption: IT WAS YOUR CHILDHOOD

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. How old were you in nineteen seventy-two, and what do you remember most? What was your favorite Saturday morning cartoon? We read every comment. Next, we're asking what made being ten years old in nineteen sixty-three so special. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: HOW OLD WERE YOU IN 1972?
